scenes.title: Cold open
narration: In 2024, breakdancer Rachael Gunn brought the garden sprinkler to the Paris Olympics, decades after its 1980s Australian origins.
This is Sprinkler dance. 1980s (revived 2010s).

Title card: Sprinkler dance · Australia / United Kingdom · 1980s (revived 2010s)

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Accounts of the dance's origins vary, with press coverage in December 2010 describing it as having originated in Australia during the 1980s alongside the era of The Bump.
Its popularity saw a massive revival when the England cricket team adopted it during their winning 2010–11 Ashes series, turning it into an internet phenomenon.

Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally used as a casual novelty, it was deployed by the England cricket team as a team bonding exercise during the Ashes series, later compared by captain Andrew Strauss to a personal version of the Māori haka.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Standing with legs slightly apart and knees slightly bent, the dancer bends their left elbow and places their left hand behind their head while outstretching the right arm inline with the shoulder.
The dancer rotates around the waist in a 180-degree sweep, pulling back three times while moving the arm to the left before swinging it back to the right in one motion.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include Paul Collingwood who introduced it to the England cricket team, Graeme Swann who documented it, and Rachael Gunn who performed it at the 2024 Paris Olympics.
Regional variants are not documented, though the movement spread globally via the internet through fan clips, vicars, choirboys, and schoolchildren.
The movement traces from 1980s Australian nightlife through to its 2010 viral revival by English cricketers and subsequent appearance in 21st-century media.
